title: Shortest One-Letter Chain
statement:
You get a word start, a word target and a list words. A chain goes from start to target one word at a time; each next word differs from the previous one in exactly one position (same length, one letter swapped). Every word after start, including target, must be in words. start itself does not have to be in the list.

Return the number of words in the shortest chain, counting both start and target. If no chain exists, return 0.

examples.why: bake → bike → dike → dime takes 3 changes, so the chain has 4 words. A longer chain through bale, male, mile and mime also exists, but the shortest one counts.
"warm" is not in the list, so no chain can end there, even though "worm" is one letter away from it.
One change. start does not need to be in the list, and the answer counts words, not changes.

constraints: start, target and every word have the same length and use lowercase letters
hints: Think of every word as a node, with an edge between two words that differ in one letter. What are you looking for in that graph?
The shortest chain is a shortest path in an unweighted graph, so use BFS from start. The number of words is the BFS level of target plus one.

Do not compare a word against every other word to find its neighbours. Instead, try changing each position to each letter a–z and look the result up in a set. Remove words from the set once they are queued.

explain.intuition:
Picture each word as a node and draw an edge between two words that differ in exactly one letter. A chain is a path, and the shortest chain is the shortest path from start to target. Every step costs the same, so BFS finds it: BFS visits nodes in order of distance, so the first time it reaches target is along a shortest route. DFS would find a chain, not the shortest one.

The cost is in finding neighbours. Comparing a word with all other words is O(N · L) per word and O(N² · L) overall. Instead, generate candidates: for each of the L positions, try all 26 letters, and keep the results that are in a hash set of the list. That is 26 · L lookups per word, independent of N. Delete a word from the set as soon as it is queued; that doubles as the visited mark and stops later levels from revisiting it.
steps: Put words in a set. If target is not in it, return 0.
Start a BFS with start at level 1.
For the current word, for each position and each letter a–z, build the changed word. If it equals target, return level + 1. If it is in the set, remove it and queue it at level + 1.
If the queue runs empty, return 0.
pitfalls: Returning the number of changes instead of the number of words. Example 3 is 2, not 1.
Forgetting that target must be in the list. In example 2 it is not, so the answer is 0 even though a close word exists.
Marking words visited when they are dequeued instead of when they are queued. The same word can then sit in the queue many times, which on 5 000 words blows up the run time.

complexity.time: O(N · L² · 26): N words, L letters, and building each candidate costs O(L)

solutions.title: BFS, comparing against every word
solutions.idea: BFS from start. A word's neighbours are found by checking every unvisited word for a one-letter difference. Simple, but O(N²) comparisons.

solutions.title: BFS, trying every one-letter change
solutions.idea: Keep the unvisited words in a set. For each word, swap each position to each letter and look the result up. Remove words from the set as they are queued.

solutions.title: BFS over wildcard buckets
solutions.idea: Group words by patterns like "b*ke": two words are one apart exactly when they share a pattern. Each bucket is emptied the first time it is used, so no pair is compared twice.

followups: Run the BFS from both ends at once and always expand the smaller frontier. Why does that cut the work so much on large lists?
Return every shortest chain, not just the length. What extra information must BFS record?
